title: Can AI forecast demand better than last year plus growth?
description: We tested AI against last year plus growth on 2,524 items. See where it wins, what tools cost, and how to test one before you buy.
verdict: AI cut error about 40% versus last year plus growth in our test. Simple statistics got most of that.[^1][^2]
AI helps most on fast, erratic items and least on slow, lumpy ones. Sort items by demand pattern first.[^3][^4]
Planner overrides help only when large and backed by news. Small or upward tweaks usually make forecasts worse.[^5][^6]
Test any model on your own history before you buy. Vendor accuracy claims use their own baselines.[^7][^8]
Price the gain in safety stock, your buffer against forecast error. Less error frees cash at the same service level.[^9][^10]

summary: AI demand forecasting predicts sales by item and week from your history and drivers like price and season.[^2][^11] Your planner reviews it before it sets the monthly plan and how much buffer stock you carry.[^12][^13] Clean history, and overrides made only with real news, make or break it.[^14][^6]
humanRole: Demand planner: owns the final number and every override, with a written reason for each. Forecasting texts say to adjust sparingly and document why.[^15][^7]
Sales and marketing: flag promotions, new accounts and lost customers. In one study, the best setup had people flag events and the model size them.[^16]
Supply or inventory planner: picks the service level, meaning how often you accept running out. The model only supplies the error spread that sizes safety stock, your buffer against error.[^13][^9]
COO or owner: approves the monthly plan at the executive S&OP (sales and operations planning) meeting.[^12][^13] ASCM's 2026 AI report advises keeping complex planning under human oversight.[^17]
teamAfter: Planners stop building numbers and start reviewing exceptions.[^7] Forecast value added (FVA) scores each step against a naive forecast, such as same week last year, and keeps only steps that help.[^18][^19]
Planner time goes to the few big calls: a promotion, a new customer, a lost account.[^16] At one European retailer, planner changes to 30 million AI forecasts added no accuracy on average.[^20]
S&OP prep shifts to scenarios and supply trade-offs, the steps that come after the forecast.[^12] ASCM advises keeping those complex planning calls with people.[^17]
Most firms keep their people. Where AI changed tasks, 66% of firms only used it to help staff, and 2% reported employment falling.[^21][^22]

example.input: Illustrative example, not a client. A 120-person industrial distributor has 6,000 active items and one warehouse, and forecasts in Excel as same month last year plus 5%. It feeds the model three years of weekly shipments per item, stockout days, open orders, prices, the promo calendar and supplier lead times.[^23][^14]
example.output: The model sorts items into four demand patterns, from steady sellers to lumpy ones, and forecasts 13 weeks ahead with a range.[^3][^2] It flags the items where last month's override hurt accuracy, and resets safety stock at the planner's chosen service level.[^7][^13] The planner reviews those flags, sales adds known events, and the monthly S&OP meeting approves the plan.[^16][^12]

recipes.name: 1. Small team on Excel (under about 2,000 items, one buyer)
recipes.when: One buyer or planner, forecasts in a spreadsheet, and no planning tool yet. Excel is still the most used forecasting tool.[^38]
flow: Buyer: export 2-3 years of weekly sales by item, with stockout weeks marked[^23][^14]
Buyer: build an Excel FORECAST.ETS baseline next to last year plus growth[^26]
Ops lead: score both on the latest 13 weeks you held back, using the test below[^39]
Buyer: trial one low-cost tool on the same held-back weeks[^24][^27]
Owner: approve only if the safety stock dollars freed beat the fee[^13]
recipes.cost: Excel's baseline is included.[^26] Forecast Pro 100 is $1,995 a year, and StockTrim is $298 a month at $3-5M revenue (prices read 26 Nov 2026).[^27][^24]

recipes.name: 2. Mid-size firm on an ERP (about 2,000-20,000 items, a demand planner)
recipes.when: A distributor or manufacturer on Dynamics 365, Business Central, NetSuite or Cin7, with a planner who owns the number.[^25][^31]
flow: Demand planner: sort items by pattern: smooth (steady), erratic (sells often, swings a lot), intermittent (often zero) and lumpy (often zero, then big)[^3]
IT or ERP admin: switch on the forecasting module or add-on in a test company[^29][^31]
Demand planner: test it on 13-26 held-back weeks from several start dates[^39]
Supply planner: recompute safety stock from the new error spread[^9][^10]
S&OP process owner: run two monthly cycles beside the old forecast[^12]
COO or owner: decide at the executive S&OP meeting[^12][^13]
recipes.cost: Dynamics 365 Supply Chain Premium is $300 per user a month, needed only for planner seats.[^25][^30] Rand Group's Business Central app is $3,500 a year plus $2,400 for AI forecasting; NetSuite and Cin7 don't publish forecasting prices.[^31][^32][^28]

recipes.name: 3. Data-led build (customer sell-through or EDI data the vendors don't see)
recipes.when: You have an analyst and data a vendor won't use, like customer point-of-sale or EDI (electronic order) feeds. In one 2026 study, retailer data cut error 44.7% against shipments alone.[^40]
flow: Analyst: build the baselines: same week last year, exponential smoothing and Croston[^2][^3]
Analyst: add one gradient-boosted model across all items, with recent sales, calendar and price[^2]
Demand planner: review forecast value added every month[^7]
Head of supply chain: keep the model only for demand patterns where it beats the baselines[^4]
recipes.cost: The libraries are free, and our 2,524-item test ran in about 7 minutes on a 4-core cloud machine.[^1] The real cost is staff time, and internal builds succeed about half as often as bought tools.[^41]

ownData.title: How much better than last year plus growth is an AI forecast?
ownData.intro: On 26 Nov 2026 we backtested six forecasting methods on public Walmart sales data from the M5 competition.[^1][^2] We summed 2,524 items across 10 stores, like one warehouse, and forecast May 2015 to May 2016 from four start dates.[^39] Error is WAPE: units missed divided by units sold, so lower is better.[^42]
rows: Bias, warehouse level (minus means too low)
Share of items where the method was best
ownData.note: Retail sales are smoother than many B2B order books, and we gave the models no promotion inputs.[^1][^2] The AI model was lightly tuned, we used an item-level growth rate, and we did not test new items or stock dollars. Simple smoothing got most of the gain: AI added 1.3 points at warehouse level and 2.8 at one store.

howToTest: Record your before numbers: today's forecast error, bias, fill rate and safety stock dollars. Score your current method on the same weeks you test the tools on.
Pull 2-3 years of weekly demand by item; two years is the minimum to learn seasons.[^23][^43] Use orders, not shipments, where you can, and mark stockout weeks.[^14]
Pick one warehouse or product family, and hold back its latest 13-26 weeks to forecast from several start dates. Never score a model on weeks it trained on.[^39]
Set three baselines: same week last year, last year plus growth, and Excel's FORECAST.ETS.[^19][^26] A tool must beat these to earn its fee.[^7]
Score with WAPE and bias (whether you run high or low), not MAPE, which breaks on zero-sales weeks.[^44][^42] Weight by dollars if a few items matter most.
Split results by demand pattern: smooth, erratic, intermittent and lumpy.[^3] Expect the biggest gains on steady and erratic sellers.[^2][^4]
Run forecast value added on your overrides: naive, then system forecast, then the planner's final number.[^7][^18] Stop the kinds of override that cost accuracy.[^6]
Price the lift in dollars: safety stock scales with error spread, so 10% less spread frees about 10% of safety stock.[^9][^10] Multiply by unit cost and your yearly carrying-cost rate.
Make each vendor run the same test on your data and hold-out before you sign. Published accuracy, like one vendor's 32% average error cut, uses that vendor's own baseline.[^8][^7]
watchOuts: Stockouts hide real demand, so the forecast drifts down and the next order shrinks.[^14][^45] Record stockout days; recovering lost demand cut WAPE from 31.75% to 29.02% in one study.[^46]
Small and upward overrides add optimism and error.[^5][^6] Require a reason code, track FVA by planner, and allow only large, news-backed changes.[^15][^7]
Growth rates on single items amplify noise. In our test, an item-level growth rate (last 13 weeks against a year earlier) raised error from 37.0% to 43.1%.[^1][^19]
A good error score can hide a forecast that runs low: our AI model was 6% under, against 1.9% for smoothing.[^1] Track bias next to error, because low forecasts mean stockouts.[^13]
The model trusts the past when the world shifts: Zillow shut its home-buying arm after a $304.4M write-down.[^47][^48] Watch error weekly, and let planners pause the model after a shock.
Services can close: AWS shut Amazon Forecast to new customers on 29 Jul 2024.[^49][^50] Keep your data, baselines and test set in-house so you can switch.

faq.q: Is AI actually useful for demand forecasting, or mostly hype?
faq.a: Useful, mostly on steady and erratic fast sellers. In our backtest AI cut error about 40% against last year plus growth, but plain smoothing got most of that.[^1] In the M5 competition, gains at the item level averaged about 3%.[^2]

faq.q: Do we need to hire a data scientist?
faq.a: Not to buy. Tools like StockTrim and ERP add-ons ship with built-in models.[^24][^31] You need one to build your own, and internal builds succeed less often.[^41]

faq.q: How much sales history do we need?
faq.a: Two years minimum to learn seasons, and three is better.[^23][^43] New items need forecasts borrowed from similar items, or judgment.[^23]

faq.q: Can we run S&OP in Excel?
faq.a: Yes. S&OP is a monthly meeting process, not a tool.[^12][^13] Excel is the most used forecasting tool in supply chains.[^38]

faq.q: What does demand forecasting software cost?
faq.a: From free in Excel, to $1,995 a year for Forecast Pro 100, to $300 per planner a month for Dynamics 365 Premium.[^26][^27][^25] We read these on vendor pages on 26 Nov 2026; Cin7's add-on, NetSuite and Flieber publish no price.[^28][^32][^34]

faq.q: How do planners override the forecast without making it worse?
faq.a: Rarely, with a written reason, and measure each override's value added.[^15][^7] Large, downward, news-backed changes tend to help; small upward ones hurt.[^5][^6]

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy when you have no data person and your items sell in common patterns. Most firms now buy: 76% of enterprise AI uses are bought, and bought tools succeed about twice as often.[^51][^41] Start with your ERP's module or add-on, tested against Excel's free baseline.[^31][^26]
buyVsBuild.build: Build when your data is the edge, such as customer sell-through or EDI orders a vendor won't use. Retailer data cut error 44.7% in one 2026 study.[^40] Keep baselines and data pipelines in-house, because managed services can close.[^49]

pickElse: Mostly new items, or under two years of history: forecast from similar items and judgment, not machine learning.[^23][^43]
Slow, lumpy spare parts: use exponential smoothing, Croston's method or a reorder point.[^4][^3] In our backtest, smoothing beat AI on lumpy items.[^1]
Make-to-order or contract demand: plan from customer orders and agreed schedules, or ask customers for their own forecast.[^40]
Few items with steady demand: Excel's FORECAST.ETS may be enough.[^26] Check it with step 3 of the test above.

offer.heading: Is your forecast beating last year plus growth?
offer.body: Bring your forecasting process and two years of weekly sales. In 30 minutes you leave with a plan to test models on your own history before you buy, and a before-and-after measure. No sales pitch.

reviews.notes: Wanted a before-and-after measure and a sense of time. The test now opens with a step that records today's error, bias, fill rate and safety stock dollars as the before numbers. Recipe 2 runs two monthly S&OP cycles in parallel, which dates the decision. Every recipe step already names its role.

Stalled on smooth, erratic, intermittent and lumpy. Recipe 2 now defines each in plain words, and the example says the patterns run from steady to lumpy. WAPE, bias, FVA, service level, safety stock, naive forecast, Croston and gradient boosting were already defined on first use.

Asked whether one site can pilot first and how it hits the unit's numbers. The hold-out step now starts with one warehouse or product family. The dollar step prices freed safety stock with unit cost and carrying-cost rate, and the before numbers include fill rate.

The head of supply chain asked how 'last year plus growth' was built and whether retail data says anything about B2B. The growth watch-out now defines the item-level growth rate, and the own-data note says we used it and that retail demand is smoother than B2B order books. The 6% under-forecast stays in the table and a watch-out, since it hits fill rate.

Steve could tell in seconds what the page answers, and liked that every tool row shows a price or says none is published. He wanted the hard part named and what the 30 minutes buys. The On this page list now calls testing on your own history the hard part, and the offer promises a test plan and a before-and-after measure, with no pitch. The research had no sourced facts on data security, so the page makes no claims there.
